terms.definition: Virtual Private Cloud — a logically isolated network within AWS where you deploy resources. Think of it as your private section of the AWS cloud with its own IP range and security rules.
terms.example: Like a walled school campus inside a large city — only authorized people can enter.

terms.definition: A subdivision of a VPC within a single Availability Zone. Subnets segment your VPC into smaller address blocks for organizational or security purposes.
terms.example: Like different floors in a school — the science wing, admin wing, and library each with their own purpose.

terms.definition: Classless Inter-Domain Routing — notation for specifying IP address ranges. Written as IP/prefix-length (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16).
terms.example: 10.0.0.0/16 means 65,536 IP addresses starting from 10.0.0.0.

terms.definition: A VPC component that enables bidirectional communication between a VPC and the internet. Must be attached to the VPC and referenced in a route table.
terms.example: Like the main entrance gate of a school — both visitors can enter and students can leave.

terms.definition: A set of rules (routes) that determine where network traffic from a subnet or VPC is directed.
terms.example: Like a GPS or directory — tells each packet which door to go through to reach its destination.

terms.definition: Network Access Control List — a stateless, optional firewall at the subnet level that evaluates inbound and outbound rules independently for every packet.
terms.example: Like a checkpoint at each floor entrance — every person entering AND leaving is checked separately.

terms.definition: A stateful, virtual firewall at the instance level. Only supports allow rules; return traffic is automatically permitted for allowed inbound connections.
terms.example: Like a lock on each classroom door — only people with the right key can enter, and they can leave freely.

terms.definition: A firewall property where each packet is evaluated independently without remembering previous connections. NACLs are stateless.
terms.example: A stateless guard checks your ID every time you enter AND every time you leave, even if they just saw you.

terms.definition: A firewall property where return traffic for an allowed connection is automatically permitted without a separate rule. Security Groups are stateful.
terms.example: A stateful guard remembers you came in, so they automatically let you out without checking your ID again.

terms.definition: Temporary, randomly assigned high-numbered ports (1024-65535) used for return traffic in TCP connections. NACLs must explicitly allow these for responses to reach clients.
terms.example: When you SSH into a server, your laptop picks a random high port (like 50231) for the server's response to come back to.

terms.definition: A subnet whose associated route table has a route to an Internet Gateway, allowing resources inside to communicate with the internet.
terms.example: The wing of the school that faces the main street — visitors can approach directly.

terms.definition: A subnet whose route table has no route to an Internet Gateway, keeping resources isolated from direct internet access.
terms.example: The secure server room in the school — no one from outside can reach it directly.

terms.definition: The VPC that AWS automatically creates in each region when you open a new account. It is pre-configured for quick use but not recommended for production.
terms.example: Like a furnished apartment AWS gives you to get started — convenient but not customized for your needs.

terms.definition: Internet Protocol version 4 — uses 32-bit addresses written in dotted decimal notation (e.g., 192.168.1.1). Provides approximately 4.3 billion unique addresses.
terms.example: 192.168.0.1 is an IPv4 address — four numbers from 0-255 separated by dots.

terms.definition: Internet Protocol version 6 — uses 128-bit addresses in hexadecimal notation. Provides virtually unlimited addresses to solve IPv4 exhaustion.
terms.example: 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334 is an IPv6 address.

terms.definition: An IP address that is globally routable and reachable from anywhere on the internet. EC2 instances in public subnets can be assigned public IPs.
terms.example: Your EC2's public IP 54.210.x.x that you use to SSH into it from your laptop.

terms.definition: An IP address in reserved non-routable ranges (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x) that can only be used within a private network.
terms.example: Your EC2's internal IP 10.0.1.45 that other resources in the VPC use to communicate with it.

terms.definition: A physically distinct data center (or cluster of data centers) within an AWS region. Each subnet lives in exactly one AZ.
terms.example: ap-south-1a, ap-south-1b are two AZs in the Mumbai region — separate buildings with independent power and network.

terms.definition: A managed AWS service that allows resources in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet, while blocking inbound connections initiated from the internet.
terms.example: Like a mail room — private office staff can send letters out, but no one outside can walk directly to the private offices.

terms.definition: A static, public IPv4 address that you can allocate and assign to AWS resources. Unlike auto-assigned public IPs, Elastic IPs persist even after instance restarts.
terms.example: A permanent phone number for your EC2 — doesn't change when the server is restarted.
